title: The Temple's Fall and the Coming of the Son of Man
summary: As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple admires its great stones, and Jesus predicts that not one will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he tells four disciples what to expect: deceivers, wars, persecution, the abomination of desolation, a time of great distress, and the coming of the Son of Man in the clouds to gather his elect. He ends by warning that no one knows the day or hour and commanding all his followers to keep watch.
story: Jesus has spent chapters 11 and 12 in the temple, judging it by act and parable and silencing its leaders. Now he leaves it for the last time and announces its destruction. This chapter, often called the Olivet discourse, is the longest speech of Jesus in Mark, and it comes just before the passion. It looks beyond the cross to the church's future: suffering witness, the fall of Jerusalem, and the final coming of the Son of Man. Mark places it here so that readers facing persecution and upheaval would understand their own time in light of Jesus' words, and so that the following chapters, where Jesus himself is handed over, beaten, and stands before governors, show him walking the road he describes for his followers.
historical:
Herod the Great's rebuilding of the temple made it one of the wonders of the Roman world. Josephus, the Jewish historian, describes its white stone and gold, and some of the Herodian blocks still visible in the western retaining wall of the temple mount weigh many tons. In AD 66 the Jews of Judea revolted against Rome. After years of war and bitter internal conflict, the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem, and in AD 70 the temple was burned and the city largely destroyed. The fourth-century church historian Eusebius records a tradition that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a revelation, left the city before the siege and settled at Pella, east of the Jordan.

The phrase abomination of desolation comes from Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11) and in its first setting pointed to the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up a pagan altar in the temple and stopped the daily sacrifices; the book of 1 Maccabees uses the same phrase for that event. Jewish memory of that desecration was vivid, and in AD 40 the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered his statue placed in the temple, provoking a crisis that ended only with his death. Mark's parenthesis, let the reader understand, suggests his readers knew that the words had a sharp meaning in their own day.
cultural:
The chapter is written in the language of Jewish apocalyptic, a style of writing found in Daniel and in many Jewish works of the period. Apocalyptic writing describes God's decisive acts in history using cosmic imagery: the sun darkened, stars falling, heavens shaken. The prophets used the same language for the fall of empires in their own time; Isaiah 13:10 applies it to Babylon's fall and Isaiah 34:4 to judgment on Edom. Readers should not assume it is either purely literal astronomy or mere metaphor; it announces events of world-shaking significance with God behind them.

The practical instructions fit Judea: flat roofs reached by outside stairs, which is why someone on the housetop should not go back inside; field workers who left their outer cloak at the edge of the field; winter rains that made wadis impassable and flight difficult. Birth pains were a common Jewish image for the sufferings expected before God's new age. The night was divided into four watches by Roman reckoning, and verse 35 names them: evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and morning. The doorkeeper was the servant charged with watching for the master's return.
literary: The discourse answers the disciples' two-part question (verse 4), when will these things happen and what will be the sign, and it is built around repeated commands: see to it, be on your guard, keep watch. The first section (5 to 13) warns against deception and describes persecution and witness, which are the beginning, not the end. The second (14 to 23) describes a crisis in Judea centered on the abomination of desolation. The third (24 to 27) moves to the cosmic coming of the Son of Man, drawing on Daniel 7:13. The fourth (28 to 37) gives two parables, the fig tree and the doorkeeper, and holds in tension two statements: these things will happen within this generation (verse 30), and no one knows that day or hour (verse 32). The final word, “Keep watch!” is addressed to everyone. The chapter's warning to stay awake sets up Gethsemane in chapter 14, where the disciples fall asleep three times.

outline.t: The beginning of birth pains: deception, war, and persecution
The abomination of desolation and the great distress
The coming of the Son of Man
The lesson of the fig tree
No one knows the day or hour: keep watch

doctrines.note: The Son of Man will come in the clouds with great power and glory and gather his elect from the ends of the earth. The church's hope is not that history will simply improve, but that Christ will return to complete what he began.

Jesus tells his followers plainly that they will be handed over, beaten, betrayed by family, and hated because of his name. Suffering is not a sign that God has lost control; it is the setting in which the gospel is proclaimed and the Spirit gives words.

Before the end, the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations (verse 10). Persecution before governors and kings becomes an occasion of witness, and the church's calling in the time of waiting is to tell the news, not to calculate dates.

The temple's destruction is presented as God's judgment on a city and house that rejected his Son, in continuity with the prophets' warnings. It is also a foretaste and sign of the final judgment when the Son of Man comes.

words.note: Gregoreo, to stay awake, keep watch. It appears three times in the closing verses and three more in Gethsemane (14:34, 37, 38), where the disciples fail to do it. Watching in Mark is not scanning the news for signs; it is faithful alertness, doing one's assigned task while the master is away.

Bdelugma, abomination, something detestable, especially an idol or pagan rite that defiles what is holy. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew word for idolatrous practices. Joined with desolation, it names a sacrilege that leaves the sanctuary empty of true worship.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, tribulation. The word's basic image is being crushed or pressed. The New Testament uses it for the ordinary sufferings of believers (Acts 14:22) and for the great distress Jesus describes here, days unmatched since creation.

Eklektos, chosen or elect. It describes the people God has chosen for himself, a title given to Israel in the Old Testament and here to Jesus' followers. God shortens the days for their sake, guards them from deception, and gathers them at the end. Election in this chapter is a comfort for the persecuted, not a puzzle for the curious.

christ: In this chapter Jesus speaks as the prophet who foretells the future and as the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom. He claims that his words are more permanent than heaven and earth (verse 31), language the Old Testament uses of God's word (Isaiah 40:8). At the same time, he says the Son does not know the day or hour, a statement the church has understood as part of his real human limitation in his earthly life, without denying his full deity. The temple he predicts will fall is being replaced by himself: his own death and resurrection will be the new center of God's presence among his people. The persecution he describes for his disciples, being handed over, beaten, and brought before governors, is the road he himself walks in the next two chapters.

hard.q: Jesus said this generation would not pass away until all these things happened. Was he mistaken about the timing of his return?
hard.a: Verse 30 is one of the most discussed sayings in the Gospels. Some critical scholars read it as a prediction that the world would end within the lifetime of Jesus' hearers, and conclude that it was not fulfilled. Christian interpreters have offered several other readings. The preterist view holds that the whole discourse, including the coming of the Son of Man, refers to the events of AD 70, reading the cosmic language as prophetic imagery for the fall of Jerusalem and the vindication of Jesus, and so the generation saw it all. The futurist view takes much of the chapter to describe events still ahead, and reads generation as a race or kind of people rather than the people then alive. A widely held mixed view sees the chapter as answering two questions: these things in verse 30 are the temple's destruction and its signs, which happened within a generation, while that day in verse 32 is the final coming, whose time no one knows. Each position has able defenders, and the timing of Christ's return is a question on which faithful readers differ. What all agree on is the chapter's own emphasis: do not be deceived, persevere, and keep watch.

questions: The disciple admired the temple's stones, and Jesus said they would fall. What impressive things in your life or culture feel permanent but are not?
Jesus warns repeatedly against being deceived by people who claim to speak in his name. How can you tell the difference between faithful watchfulness and anxious speculation about the end?
Each servant in the parable has an assigned task while the master is away. What is the task God has given you to do faithfully while you wait?
